tasks.title: Key login instead of a password
tasks.statement: The server lets user alice in with the password alice123, and that is enough for bots. Switch to keys. On the PC create a key (`ssh-keygen`), copy it to the server (`ssh-copy-id -P alice123 alice@192.168.0.20`; the password is needed once), check the key login, and then turn off password login on the server (`sshd password off`).
tasks.hint: Order matters: first the key and the copy, then disabling passwords — otherwise you lock yourself out. Check: `ssh alice@192.168.0.20` logs in with the key, `ssh -o PubkeyAuthentication=no -P alice123 alice@192.168.0.20` is refused.

tasks.title: The host key has changed
tasks.statement: After the server was reinstalled (the administrator confirmed that the key change was planned), login shows “REMOTE HOST IDENTIFICATION HAS CHANGED”. The client's known_hosts still holds the old key. Remove the stale entry for 192.168.0.20 (`ssh-keygen -R 192.168.0.20`) and log in again — the client will remember the new key.
tasks.hint: `ssh-keygen -R 192.168.0.20`, then `ssh alice@192.168.0.20`. Do not turn host key checking off permanently: it protects against server impersonation.

tasks.title: Bastion: logging in to the internal network
tasks.statement: The server 10.0.2.20 in the internal network is reachable over SSH only from the bastion 10.0.1.5 — that is how the firewall is set up. It is not reachable directly from the PC. Set up the login `ssh -J alice@10.0.1.5 alice@10.0.2.20` (the client key already exists): authorize the PC key (`ssh-keygen -l` shows the fingerprint) both on the bastion and on the internal server for user alice. Password login is off there.
tasks.hint: `ssh-keygen -l` on the PC → fingerprint. On the bastion and on the internal server: `sshd authorize alice <fingerprint>`. Then `ssh -J alice@10.0.1.5 alice@10.0.2.20`.

spec_text./goals/0/text: Login to the internal server through the bastion
spec_text./goals/1/text: The internal server is closed directly from the PC

tasks.title: VPN between two offices
tasks.statement: Offices A (192.168.1.0/24) and B (192.168.2.0/24) are connected only through the internet, and the internet does not route private addresses. Build a tunnel between the gateways: on gateway A the peer is 198.51.100.1 and the tunnel address is 10.9.0.1/30; on gateway B the peer is 203.0.113.1 and the address is 10.9.0.2/30; the shared secret is the same on both. Then add routes to the remote networks through the tunnel.
tasks.hint: `vpn add wg0 --peer 198.51.100.1 --address 10.9.0.1/30 --key s3cr3t` on A and `vpn add wg0 --peer 203.0.113.1 --address 10.9.0.2/30 --key s3cr3t` on B. Routes: on A `ip route add 192.168.2.0/24 dev wg0`, on B `ip route add 192.168.1.0/24 dev wg0`. Press ▶ and find the “tunnel wg0” encapsulation in the log.

spec_text./goals/0/text: PC A reaches PC B (private addresses across the internet)
spec_text./goals/2/text: Traffic between the offices goes through the gateways via the tunnel

tasks.title: Split tunnel
tasks.statement: An employee's laptop at home: the tunnel to the corporate gateway is already up, but the default route points into the tunnel — all internet traffic goes through the office, and the tunnel itself has lost its path to the peer (ping to the corporate network fails). Set up a split tunnel: the corporate network 10.0.0.0/8 goes into the tunnel (wg0), everything else goes directly through the home router 192.168.100.1.
tasks.hint: `ip route del default`, then `ip route add default via 192.168.100.1` and `ip route add 10.0.0.0/8 dev wg0`. Check: ping 10.0.0.5 goes through the corporate gateway, ping 198.51.100.10 does not.

spec_text./goals/0/text: Corporate server 10.0.0.5 is reachable through the tunnel
spec_text./goals/1/text: The public website goes directly, bypassing the corporate gateway
